newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 27.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- NEWMAN TONKS MOUNTS DEFENCE

Hardware group Newman Tonks is expected to post its key defence document to shareholders this week. The company hopes to convince a sceptical stock market that FKI's current 200 million stg shares and cash bid undervalues Newman's scope for recovery. The main defence will be a profit forecast with pre-tax profits estimated at close to 18 million stg for
1996, ahead of forecasts of 16 million stg before the bid.
-- SATELLITE TV FIRM ATTACKS FAILURE TO LIST SHARES

Greenwich Communications, distributor of satellite television equipment in Portugal and which has not made a profit for 10 years, has criticised the Stock Exchange for refusing to admit its shares. The company was delisted last month after the closure of the Unlisted Securities Market. Alfred Stirling, chairman, said that he could see no reason why the Exchange should refuse entry to a company which made a loss of 57,000 stg from sales of 152,000 stg in its last reported accounts.
-- BA RENEWS JET ORDER TALKS

British Airways has re-opened talks with manufacturers, Boeing, McDonnell Douglas and Avro, about buying 30 aircraft for a new regional jet fleet at a cost of $500 million. This comes after finalising the outlines of a cost and pay cut agreement with the majority of 2,000 staff on the regional payroll. BA said that if it could conclude negotiations with staff groups which had agreed to its efforts to bring pay and costs more closely into line with market rates, main board approval would be sought in the summer to replace the fleet.
THE TIMES
-- BANKS LOOK AT WILLIAM HILL DISPOSAL PLANS

Close Brothers, Brent Walker's merchant bank, have drawn up plans to realise the value of its 1,700 William Hill chain of betting shops. The bank is reviewing options for William Hill including a straight sale, a stock market flotation, and a plan to reverse the chain into the old Brent Walker name and use the tax losses available to the business. Brent Walker is also planning to pursue its six-year lawsuit with Grand Metropolitan from whom it bought William Hill over allegations that profits had been overstated to inflate the purchase price.
-- GROWTH FIGURES HOLD KEY TO RISE IN INTEREST RATES

Surveys by Reuters and MMS International have found that the markets are looking for gross domestic product to have risen by 0.8 percent in the final three months of last year, stronger than the 0.7 percent recorded in the third quarter. A string of disappointing economic data recently has cast doubt on whether growth will be as strong as the market consensus suggests, including a decline of 0.5 percent in manufacturing output in November and a 0.8 percent fall in retail sales in December. These figures hold the key on whether Chancellor Kenneth Clarke will rise base rates before an election.
-- FORMER LEEDS UNITED DIRECTOR TO SUE FOR FEES

Former Leeds United director, Peter Gilman, is to sue Caspian Group, the club's new owner, for unpaid legal fees of 13,750 stg, which he claims he incurred taking independent advise as was required under the City code on takeovers and mergers. He says he was indemnified against these costs by Leeds United and that the club is bound to pay him. He will also attempt to have a libel action against him thrown out of court.
THE GUARDIAN
-- CLARKE SEEKS TO ALLAY RATE RIFT FEARS

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has said that he is united with Governor of the Bank of England, Eddie George, in the battle against inflation. George is preparing to renew his call for dearer borrowing but the City believes an increase before the election is unlikely. The Bank will underline its view that a delay in tightening policy would be a mistake in next month's quarterly Inflation Report, which will stress that the stronger pound does not provide an adequate bulwark against price pressures in the domestic economy.
-- NO WINNERS AS GROCERS FIGHT IT OUT

According to retail consultants Verdict Research, thousands of jobs in food retailing will be put at risk if the battle for supremacy among Britain's supermarkets triggers a full-scale price war. The report says that the problems at Sainsbury's, with its third profit warning in four years, could lead to a battle among the grocery chains which will slash food bills for customers and could threaten smaller outlets.
-- AFFIDAVITS 'SHOW HORLICK'S PLANS'

Despite statements in affidavits sworn by members at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Nicola Horlick insists her talks with Dutch investment bank ABN Amro were "purely informal and preliminary". Allegations have emerged at the weekend that the Dutch bank planned to recruit Horlick and her team of investment managers from Morgan. Her colleagues are said to have claimed she was shown a business plan by London head of Amro, Nick Bannister. One of the options he is alleged to have shown her was for ABN to sign up all the key staff at Morgan Grenfell Investment Management.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- PROMISING AIDS TRIALS PROVIDE A SHOT IN THE ARM FOR GLAXO

Glaxo Wellcome's fortunes are set to increase with promising Aids trials results. The company said it is "encouraged by these initial reports" even if it is too early to draw firm conclusions from a small trial. Glaxo claim that a majority of patients suffering from human immunodeficiency virus saw levels of the virus drop to undetectable levels following four weeks of treatment with new compounds under development.
-- UTILITIES TAX SEEN AS 'TIP OF ICEBERG'

Julian Fosh, investment director with Scottish Amicable Investment Managers, claims that Labour's plans to raise up to 10 billion stg from a one-off windfall tax on the privatised utilities is only "the tip of the iceberg". He claims there could be "severe downward pressure" on the share price of the utilities from tighter regulation and increased competition, regardless of the outcome of the general election.
-- CABLE AND WIRELESS POISED TO GIVE MERCURY THE BOOT

Cable and Wireless has taken its first step in removing the "Mercury" brand name from its UK telephone subsidiary's London headquarters by concealing the corporate logo on the front of the building behind white boards. The move is a step to incorporating Mercury in a five billion stg merger with three cable operators. The move confirms the drive by Dick Brown, Cable and Wireless's chief executive, towards "global branding", using the C&W identity in all its subsidiaries.
